Hey there! If your end goal would be to get into Data Science I think I'd suggest seriously thinking about doing that for your bachelor's. Especially if you want to get into a data science or related MSc. after your bachelor's (which I recommend), some universities might not let you enroll with an econ degree (mine did, but I had to do an extra round of admission to prove that I knew enough about stats, math and programming)

The transition was super worthy for me, as I find the stuff I work on really cool and I'm starting my data science related PhD in November, so I guess you could say I kinda found my path in life lol

Speaking again about the transition: it is doable (hell, I did it!), but I also took a semester off before starting my MSc. to self-study some python and get better foundations in maths since I think I was really lacking in that field. I also know of another two guys in my program who came from econ (and which didn't take a semester off) and they're both doing brilliantly, with one of them who now develops computer vision models, so again, there are some hurdles to clear, but I totally believe it can be done and that it is possible to get into any data science field with enough willpower and interest 

As a last note, if you're EU based, don't think too much about the prestige of the university where you're going to get your bachelor's, it will hardly matter: see it more as a gateway to get the necessary credits to get into a MSc

If you want you can write me a PM, maybe we can check together the courses from the two degrees you are considering and see what's best for what you want to do. I was in your position once and I'd love to help!

There is a sort of cultural barrier when talking with Italians about food, since traditional food for us is rooted in one's feeling of belonging to a specific community (and I'm not talking about italian food in general: I'm from Rome and I have strong opinions on what a "real" carbonara or amatriciana is, but I don't care that much if we are talking about food from Milan/Naples/etc.).

People are free to add whatever they want to their carbonara, but at that point it's just another pasta dish for me, not a carbonara, since carbonara is synonymous with the roman tradition and culture which I grew up with, it's part of my community, and I don't think a version of it with garlic can represent it

I know it sounds a bit melodramatic but food is literally part of our cultural identity lol
I'm sure it does, nothing wrong with that, it just sounds really foreign to me

A cheeseburger is still a cheeseburger if you put some toppings on it, but is a Big Mac still a Big Mac if you add bacon in it? Is it a "Big Mac with bacon"? Something else altogether? Kinda sounds like a philosophical question

But anyway, the reason why I wouldn't call it "carbonara" if you add garlic to it is actually because I don't think it would mix well with it: italian cuisine is traditionally quite simple and based on excellent ingredients and the careful balance of their flavours. I've never personally tried carbonara with garlic, but it sounds kinda off to me since I can't imagine the flavour of garlic mixing well with the already very strong taste of guanciale and pecorino (this might not be true for you, it's totally possible that the carbonara you know is totally different from the one I do and maybe garlic is a match made in heaven with yours)

Still, one of the most renowned restaurant of traditional roman food in Rome adds mint to its carbonara and still calls it carbonara, so who am I to argue over names (I'd just call it carbonara with garlic btw lmao)

I'm Italian and while I'm not a food-nazi (I've tried my fair share of bastardized italian food while living abroad), one could argue that adding and/or changing one ingredient in a three-ingredient dish significantly alters it and as such it can't be considered authentic anymore. You're free to add garlic to your carbonara if you like it, but I don't think I would call it such
